scenario.name: CISA AA24-242A, Symantec & Mandiant — RansomHub Ransomware: Kaspersky TDSSKiller / EDRKillShifter BYOVD, Safe-Mode Boot & Curve25519 Encryption
scenario.overview: Imagine a neighborhood auto repair garage with a wide roll-up shutter bay, a red rolling tool chest, spare tire racks, and a twin-post hydraulic car lift raising a sedan off the floor. Rolling a familiar customer sedan into the repair garage bay, a rogue mechanic hits the hydraulic switch to lift the car high above the concrete floor. In this real-world scenario, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the garage roll-up service door in tiny disguised batches, then smuggles copied records out past the garage roll-up service door in tiny disguised batches. During the next routine safety inspection, the shop foreman raises the sedan on the lift and spots the unrecorded aftermarket wire bolted beneath the frame. In this scenario (T1562.001, CISA AA24-242A, Symantec & Mandiant, RansomHub Ransomware: Kaspersky TDSSKiller / EDRKillShifter BYOVD, Safe-Mode Boot & Curve25519 Encryption), the attacker follows one continuous intrusion path so each later Step can show the exact handoff that makes the next stage possible. The attack unfolds in one continuous arc: signed TDSSKiller.exe, then safe-Mode RunOnce Persistence, then sHA-256 -pass Config Decryption. Steps #1–#3 walk that chain end-to-end by covering Signed TDSSKiller.exe, then Safe-Mode RunOnce Persistence, then SHA-256 -pass Config Decryption, while the Process Hierarchy tab keeps the Parent → Child spawn tree visible so you can see which trusted process launched the next payload. Primary detection correlates Sysmon Event 6 with the documented host and network chain.

stages.title: Stage 2: Safe-Mode RunOnce Persistence (`*safemode`) & Shadow Copy / Volume Mounting
stages.subtitle: Defense Evasion & Persistence (T1562.009 - Safe Mode Boot / T1547.001)
stages.description: Working underneath the raised chassis out of sight of the front waiting counter, the mechanic bolts a hidden bypass module directly onto the car’s starter wiring. Here in Step 2 inside the repair garage, the intruder leaves a hidden spare latch behind so they can walk back into the repair garage later without disturbing the factory sealed spare-parts rack. When -safeboot is passed, RansomHub writes its execution command (prefixed with an asterisk * in HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce, which instructs Windows to execute the key even inside Safe Mode), sets bcdedit.exe /set {current} safeboot minimal, mounts all hidden unmounted disk volumes via FindFirstVolumeW / SetVolumeMountPointW, and deletes shadow copies (logged in Sysmon Event 13 with SafeModeRegistryTrick=Asterisk-prefixed RunOnce value , *RansomHub executes in Safe Mode, BootConfigChange=bcdedit.exe /set {current} safeboot minimal, MitreTechnique=T1562.009 , Safe Mode Boot so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes reg.exe add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce" /v "*RansomHub" /t REG_SZ /d "C:\ProgramData\rhub.exe -pass 7c9e1a..." /f (which Modifies or queries Windows Registry keys and values , reg.exe add "HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce" /v "*RansomHub" /t REG_ so that manipulates persistent Windows Registry configuration or credential material , T1562.009 during "Safe-Mode RunOnce Persistence , *safemode & Shadow Copy / Volume Mounting" to establish persistence, alter system behavior, or harvest secrets). Next, the follow-up artifact bcdedit.exe /set {current} safeboot minimal && shutdown.exe /r /t 0 runs (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , bcdedit.exe /set {current} safeboot minimal && shutdown.exe /r /t 0 via bcdedit.exe, passing so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1562.009 during "Safe-Mode RunOnce Persistence , *safemode & Shadow Copy / Volume Mounting" , When -safeboot is passed, RansomHub writes its execution command , prefixed with an asterisk * in HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\RunOnce, which instructs Windows to execute the key even inside Safe Mode, sets bcdedit while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). On the diagram, follow Step #2 / Link #2 (#2→ rhub.exe / ⇠#2 ACK 13) from Node ② (#2 Perimeter Firewall & NDR Tap) to Node ③ (#3 TDSSKiller.exe / EDRKillShifter (klbg.sys)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise Volumes & S3/SMB Backups (XChaCha20)).

stages.title: Stage 3: SHA-256 `-pass` Config Decryption & Curve25519 / XChaCha20 Encryption
stages.subtitle: Impact (T1486 - Data Encrypted for Impact / T1480 - Execution Guardrails)
stages.description: Lowered back onto its wheels and washed spotless outside, the sedan drives off the garage lot carrying a hidden ignition backdoor that activates on every future start. In this final step inside the repair garage, the intruder smuggles copied records out past the garage roll-up service door in tiny disguised batches until the garage service checklist board catches the mismatch. Only when supplied the exact 64-character hex password (-pass <sha256_key>) does the RansomHub binary decrypt its internal configuration in memory (preventing sandbox detonation without the operator CLI key), clear Windows Event Logs, and encrypt local and SMB files using Curve25519 (X25519 ECDH) and XChaCha20/AES-GCM (logged in Sysmon Event 11 with RansomwareFamily=RansomHub , Knight / Cyclops Code Lineage, AntiSandboxGuardrail=Requires -pass SHA-256 CLI key to decrypt embedded JSON config, EncryptionAlgorithm=Curve25519 ECDH + XChaCha20 / AES-256 so analysts can verify the exact actor and target artifact). Under the hood, the observed step executes rhub.exe -pass 7c9e1a4b8d2f0e3a5c6b9d8e7f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d7e8f9a -network=true (which executes the technical command / telemetry directive , rhub.exe -pass 7c9e1a4b8d2f0e3a5c6b9d8e7f1a2b3c4d5e6f7a8b9c0d1e2f3a4b5c6d7e8f9a -network=tru so that advances the scenario kill-chain under MITRE T1486 during "SHA-256 -pass Config Decryption & Curve25519 / XChaCha20 Encryption" , Only when supplied the exact 64-character hex password , -pass <sha256_key> does the RansomHub binary decrypt its internal configuration in memory , preventing sandbox detonation without the operator CLI key, clear Windows Event Logs, and encrypt local and SMB files using Curve25519 , X25519 ECDH and XChaCha20/AES-GCM while generating verifiable host or network telemetry for DFIR attribution). Next, the follow-up artifact vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet && shadowcopy delete runs (which executes vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet , or WMI Win32_ShadowCopy.Delete to invoke IVssBackupComponents::DeleteSnapshots and purge all exi so that inhibits system recovery , T1486 during "SHA-256 -pass Config Decryption & Curve25519 / XChaCha20 Encryption" by destroying local disk shadow copies before or after payload execution so defenders cannot roll back encrypted files or inspect historical volume state). On the diagram, follow Step #3 / Link #3 (#3→ rhub.exe / ⇠#3 ACK 11) from Node ③ (#3 TDSSKiller.exe / EDRKillShifter (klbg.sys)) to Node ④ (#4 Endpoint (bcdedit safeboot + ransomhub.exe -pass)), monitored by Node ⑥ (#6 Enterprise Volumes & S3/SMB Backups (XChaCha20)).
